title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation carried out through AI-generated content deployed outside any legitimate platform or institution. Scammers created a fabricated news article presenting a fake interview between two real, named public figures to lend credibility to an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The AI tools here were used to produce convincing text, and potentially other media, that mimicked the appearance of legitimate journalism. The failure is not in a commercial AI product misbehaving but in AI capabilities being deliberately applied to deceive, with no institutional safeguard in a position to catch content that was never submitted to one.

The broader pattern ASIC describes shows this is not an isolated fabrication. The volume of removed scams, spanning phishing sites and fake investment platforms, points to AI lowering the cost of producing large numbers of individually convincing deceptions. Each fake article, review, or advertisement adds a layer to what ASIC calls an elaborate fake online presence, making any single piece harder for a consumer to identify as fraudulent without independent verification against official registers.

What is not established is the identity of the people responsible, the technical tools they used to generate the content, or whether any victims suffered financial loss as a result of this specific fake interview.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake article featuring an interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock circulated online, purporting to show them arguing about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred. This scam represents a growing trend that uses artificial intelligence to create deepfake content and fabricated news articles to promote illegitimate investments. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these schemes are becoming increasingly sophisticated and prevalent online.

Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams total, a 182 percent increase from the previous year. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent with 5,476 removed, while fake investment platforms saw a 151 percent increase with 7,051 taken down. Commonly impersonated Australians include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, politician Pauline Hanson, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart. Scammers build elaborate fake online presences with news articles, reviews, and ads to deceive consumers. ASIC urges people to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers before investing and check company information against ASIC's official registers.
